Walter Schirra was an American astronaut who flew in America's first three manned space programs. He was born in 1923 and had "aviation in his blood," as his father was a WW I fighter pilot and his parents were "barn stormers" in the post-war era. In December 1965, he commanded Gemini 6-A, which, after several mechanical problems, made the historic rendezvous with Gemini 7. This joint mission set five records, including the first formation flight of two space vehicles. Schirra finished his astronaut career in October 1968 by completing 163 earth orbits as Commander of Apollo 7, the first manned flight in NASA's lunar landing program. He is also a member of the Aerospace Hall of Fame and recipient of the Collier and the Harmon International Trophies. He retired from the US Navy and NASA in 1969.

persona: James Hector, a geologist who lived from 1834 to 1907, was born in Edinburgh, Scotland, and went on to pursue an eminent scientific career in New Zealand. He was educated at Edinburgh Academy and studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh before graduating in 1856. Hector was recommended by Sir Roderick Murchison to serve as the geologist on the Palliser Expedition to Canada led by John Palliser in 1857. The expedition explored new railway routes for the Canadian Pacific Railway and collected new species of plants. Hector's role in the Palliser Expedition was judged to be successful, and in 1862 he arrived in Dunedin, New Zealand with a Government remit to conduct a three-year geological survey of the south of New Zealand's South Island. In 1865, Hector was asked to establish the Geological Survey of New Zealand, which he did, with a headquarters in Wellington. He also became chief scientific adviser to the colonial government in New Zealand and, in 1868, he married Maria Georgiana Monro, the daughter of the Speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives. Hector went on to run New Zealand's most important scientific society, the New Zealand Institute, for a total of 45 years, and in 1885 he became Chancellor of the University of New Zealand. He retired from public life in 1903, having for decades controlled almost every aspect of state-funded science. Hector was not above criticism, especially for his policy of gathering Maori artefacts for the Colonial Museum, but, without doubt, he made a lasting impression on his adopted country. He died in 1907 near Wellington in New Zealand.
